I think now, when we are talking in terms of national unity, keeping our country together and upholding the regional aspirations of different sections of the land, it may be time for us, prior to any consideration of abolishing that institution, to consider amendments to the existing constitution, or changes in existing constitutional legislation which would have the effect of improving that institution, making it more responsive to the purpose for which it was first created, and in fact making the Senate of Canada a part of the over-all plan of helping the people in the different regions in Canada feel that they are participating in a Confederation worth saving. I join with that hon. member in criticizing the particular way in which the Government of Canada has regarded the Senate, and that is with the same sort of contempt with which it regards this part of the Parliament of Canada, the House of Commons. 1 join with the hon. member in his criticism of this particular tendency of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Your Honour is aware, and as the House is aware, it is not the normal practice of the Leader of the Opposition to take part in the adjournment debate; but I am doing so today because, in my view, there is a fundamental principle of the parliamentary system which is at stake here and which is being violated by the Government of Canada. The principle is that ministers of the government must take responsibility for the acts of civil servants under their general direction. That is well established in all the writing about the parliamentary system in this country and elsewhere.
I quote briefly from McGregor Dawson's basic textbook "The Government of Canada" where Professor Dawson says:
The Minister at the head of every department is responsible for everything that is done within that department.
From "Constitutional Law" by Wade and Phillips, as reproduced in H. V. Wiseman's book, "Parliament and the Executive", we find the following:
For what an unnamed official does or does not do, his Minister alone must answer in Parliament and the official, who cannot be heard in his own defence, is therefore protected from attack. The positive liability of a Minister is essential to the performance by Parliament and, more particularly, by the House of Commons of its role of critic of the Executive.
That authority goes on to make a fundamental point in this case, and that is that no minister can shield himself by blaming his official.
What we have seen far too frequently in the practices of this government is precisely the practice of blaming officials where the ministers themselves should take responsibility. We saw that in the case of Larry Stopforth, in the case of the executive assistant to the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), and now in this case we are seeing it in the case of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The House and the country know that there were illegal acts, but what we have to determine is by whom were those illegal acts committed and at whose direction. Let me come to the question of "by whom". VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN BASIC PENSION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question relates to a different matter but it is equally serious. The reason I say it is equally serious is because it involves good faith.
May I say at the outset that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) explained to me satisfactorily why it is not possible for him to be here at this time, but I trust that the message I shall try to get to him through his parlamentary secretary will be very seriously considered.
My question arises from answers that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has given both to my friend, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), and me, regarding the basic rate of the war disability pension. The history is long, but it can be put in a nutshell.
Originally the war disability pension, which was established shortly after World War 1, was related to a certain level of pay in the then civil service. Over the years it got way behind that. As a result of the Woods commission study, the matter was reviewed and in 1973, following a study by a special tripartite committee, the 100 per cent disability pension was geared to the average income of five designated levels in the public service. Therefore in 1973 we got back to where we were in the early twenties.
When that new basis was established in 1973, the urging of the tripartite committee and of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs was that that level be maintained, that as the wages of those five categories of public servants went up, the basic pension should go up accordingly. The government refused to accept that part of the recommendation, and said instead that from 1973 on the basic rate would go up in accordance with the rise in the cost of living. That, Mr. Speaker, we regarded as unfair, breaking faith with the veterans of several decades, but the government put it through.
Between 1973 and now, even with the raising of the pension according to the rise in the cost of living, there has developed a $500 a year gap between what the veterans are receiving and the average wage of those five designated groups. In other words, what we predicted in 1973, because the government refused to accept our recommendation at that time, has come true, and come true with vengeance. Our veterans today are close to $540 a year behind the counterpart average in the public service.
A year or so after the 1973 change, because of representations members like my friend and some of the rest of us were making, the government began to show interest. We had so

many favourable answers to our questions last year that the veterans of Canada thought it was going to be done. I certainly thought so. It looked to me as though we had made the point, that the Minister of Veterans Affairs would not let the veterans down.
Last Wednesday and Thursday the minister answered the two of us by saying the government haddecided not to increase the basic rate, in other words not to put it back to the standard that was accepted in 1973. As if that were not enough, refusing to make an increase, the minister made a statement which veterans across Canada feel is insulting. He said he was sure that, as good Canadians, they would accept the decision of the government and not ask for this increase in this time of restraint.
My experience with veterans' organizations is that, although they press their point, they do it with care and dignity. They refrain from using strong language. However, the word I am getting now from veterans' organizations through letters and their publications is to the effect that they have to take the gloves off. Good faith has not been kept with the veterans by the government in refusing to keep the proposal that the basic pension should be geared to the standard in those five designated groups and kept at that level.
I have every reason to believe that the minister agrees with this proposition. Last spring he told us, time and again, that it was being considered, that he was hopeful he would be able to do it. It is his colleagues in cabinet who have turned him down.
I hope he has fought his level best with the cabinet. They have done a disservice to him and a disservice to the veterans by this decision.
I know the government is in economic trouble. However, the last people the government should take its economic troubles out on are the veterans of this country. But it is doing it on the veterans, it is doing it on the senior citizens, and to my mind this is extremely serious. I am glad the veterans organizations are saying the time has come to take the gloves off. I put it to the minister, through his parliamentary secretary, that the answer he gave the week before last cannot stand.
I see some of the members on the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, including the chairman, sitting over there during this adjournment debate. I hope there will be support from all sides of the House, and that the answer the minister gave will not be allowed to stand. The veterans long ago have shown that they are good Canadians and that they deserve to have the promises made to them kept. I therefore call upon the parliamentary secretary not to try to defend what has happened but to assure the House he will put the case to the minister as strongly as he can. This battle must be won.

furniture imports have increased by 26.3 per cent last year. With regard to the changes made in the Income Tax Act concerning the individual, we see that Bill C-ll recommends an increase of $100 in the amount that can be deducted as employment expenses, raising the maximum to $250. In this regard, on March 28 last, I asked the House, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, for unanimous consent to present a motion to that effect. In short, I was asking, no more and no less, that section 8(1 )(a) of the Income Tax Act be amended to allow deduction of all travelling expenses incurred by working people to get to work and come back home using public transportation, for tax purposes, provided vouchers were filed. In my humble opinion, the $100 increase granted by the federal government is really not adequate.
Subject of course to some exemptions, most wage earners under the act as it stands can claim only up to $150, a deduction equal to 3 per cent of the income from a job, when in fact it costs them anywhere between $300 to $600 a year to get to work and come back. I sincerely feel that it would be more advantageous if most workers or wage earners generally were encouraged to use public transportation to shuttle back and forth from work because, on the one hand, it would save a whole lot of energy, and on the other, it would save hundreds of millions of dollars paid out in subsidies by the various levels of government. So, in short, with my motion of March 28 last,
1 was asking the government to allow for income tax purposes, certain tax benefits to those who have to get to work; I feel that would have had rewarding results first, as I said, by saving energy, and then, by benefitting the worker. As usual, unfortunately, the federal government did not see fit to give effect to my motion. They tend to brush aside with a flick of the hand everything that comes from the opposition.
Then, there is inflation about which I should like to say a few words. The crux of the inflation problem lies in prices. Any inquiry into the causes of the inflation in prices should start out with an in-depth study of the mechanisms of prices as they relate to our monetary system. In addition, as price setting is an integral part of the monetary system, such a survey should of necessity include a detailed examination of the operations of that system. That being recognized, one can easily wonder why the mechanism whereby prices are set is so sadly lacking in our society. It has never been updated by our own bankers.
The rigidity of the transaction pattern has revealed itself as one of the major obstacle to mankind's progress and often only

a very serious crisis or an impending catastrophe succeeds in breaking up this deadlock. It is precisely a disaster of that sort which is facing the western world today. Prices in Canada have been going up steadily for the last 19 years. It was back in 1953 that we saw the consumer price index go down for the last time. Over a long period of time we have had one very clear inclination, that is, toward the social policies of this country during a period of very easy economic times. It now takes strong leadership to change that emphasis back to free enterprise, the private sector, making very difficult decisions and running a tight ship.
I think it was Tolstoy who said the longest journey starts with one small step. At least we are seeing that now. I think those in the official opposition will agree that this is the right emphasis; however, those in the other parties may not agree.
The emphasis for some time to come will be on working through the private sector, through free enterprise, not with the government running so many activities in this country. This was signalled in the white paper "The Way Ahead" of a few months ago. It started in the March, 1977, budget and is being confirmed by the removal of controls.
Many people, including myself, would like to have seen controls removed sooner. I am prepared to accept the argument that this may be a very difficult winter in many ways and we might have regretted taking off controls now. However, in terms of getting the economy rolling, it would have been preferable if they could have been removed this fall.
There is another problem that is as difficult as running the country. I refer to the old problem of communicating with the people. We do not seem to be able to share the facts and our mutual experiences with the people back home. We must work as hard at that as running this country. I say that, in spite of televising the proceedings in this House, although that is capable of being edited just like the newspapers. Even though we find we are able to conduct our business well, we still cannot seem to get this across. There are people who still wonder.
This morning I noticed an announcement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on a subject which is due to be raised again shortly, namely, a guaranteed annual income with accompanying tax credits, the so-called negative taxation and so on.
I suggest to the minister that we should at least make a start in three needy areas. There are the low-income workers, the one-parent families, and unemployed workers between 60 and 65. We know these are serious problems. We should be looking for some better way to support these people and give them reassurance. But if this is to be the main social plan in this country, many of us are worried about it being the main disincentive. We found we had trouble with all our programs, getting the wrong effect through disincentives and so on. I hope we can work this out before getting into a general social support program.

I find when 1 get back home and talk to constituents there that there are certain things they want to know in the financial and economic area. They can be divided into two groups, the negative things, the things they really do not want, and the positive things, the things they want and are not getting. First the negative things. Why do we have to have them? Near the top of the list is the very complicated tax system. Somehow or other we must do something about this sooner or later, or we shall bog down beneath the weight of our own figures and paperwork.
I wonder how many people are able to fill out their own tax forms these days, the way they used to. The way things are now, it may be a haven for tax accountants, but the average citizen gets very little satisfaction. It is a hard nut to crack, now we have got this monster with us, but I feel it is a top priority.

I am talking about the business of collecting from beneficiaries after the death of the policyholder. But we still have the problem of the effect of any new tax law on those who use insurance policies as collateral for loans. What can we do about this? That practice is very popular, but such a provision is something which people are not accepting well.
I should like to read part of a letter 1 received from someone 1 consider to be a very concerned if somewhat overwrought constituent. He wrote:
Sorry, but perhaps there is a misunderstanding with regard to the October 25 budget. It appears that for the time being the "death tax" on life insurance is being withheld. However, there will still be tax changes affecting individuals borrowing on their policies. This is a most controversial issue since it changes the whole attitude toward the individual life insurance policy as compared with the practice which has emerged after years of study by the federal Department of Insurance as well as previous studies on life insurance. However, the big question is industrial strategy. Here I would like to give credit to my own colleagues who have worked hard on this question for several months, and perhaps do not yet have the final answers though they do have a great deal more insight. Before I wrap up my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on the record a short statement published by the Science Council of Canada. It is a statement of concern which is based on a larger background paper called "Uncertain Prospects: Canadian Manufacturing Industry, 1971-1977". If the House will bear with me, I should like to put this excerpt on the record, because I really think it says it all.
November 8, 1977

Canadian manufacturing industry is at risk and its future is uncertain. This uncertainty obviously extends into a distinct and pressing concern about our ability to employ the wide range of talents and skills that make the Canadian labour force such an exceptional national resource. Last year, Canada's deficit on manufactured goods was more than $10 billion. Nearly every branch of Canadian manufacturing displays weakness. Textiles, clothing, leather goods, consumer electronics-all are succumbing to fierce foreign competition. Many of our high technology industries have, since 1971, developed increasingly large deficits in balances of payment. The problems are long term and reflect fundamental structural deficiences.
Contrary to popular opinion, the 1960's were a period of relative decline in Canadian manufacturing. Canada did not progress by comparison with other industrial and semi-industrial countries. The seeds of our current distress were being sown in the so-called "golden era''. In the past two decades, the various policies bearing on industrial growth in Canada, while partially successful as short-term palliatives, have not helped to create a strong technological base. A superficial, stunted form of industrialization was produced by policies that created growth through import substitution.
Too many Canadian exports are actually a reflection of intracorporate transfers. Without the Auto-Pact, for instance, Canada would have practically no exports of manufactured goods. Between 1965 and 1970, the proportion of finished manufactures in total exports-a sector that provides productive employment and creates an indigenous base of engineering and scientific expertise-grew by 3.22 per cent (autos excluded). Denmark increased its proportion by 11.3 per cent, France by 5.5 per cent, Mexico by 16.8 per cent, and Sweden by 10.8 per cent. In relative terms, Canada fell seriously behind.
The responses of many businessmen to the current economic situation are indicative of current problems. Too much government control through regulation and interference in private entreprise; profit controls put forward by the AntiInflation Board; high taxes; uncertainty about nationalist sentiment and its possible policy implications; loss of competitively advantageous wage-rates relative to our major market area; stress on the part of government on the provision of social benefits as opposed to emphasis upon productivity-these are the elements that businessmen complain of as part of the poor business climate in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, tonight I would like to discuss the need for this country to process more of our raw materials to their finished state, and the use of tax incentives to bring this about.
For far too long we have been shipping out of this country a far too large proportion of our primary products to be processed to their final stages of production in other countries, which thereby gain the many advantages of employment, taxes and profits which accrue from this further processing.
We have in Canada the skilled manpower, managerial skill, cheap power, and excellent transportation facilities which are needed for this further processing, and it is about time we started doing something about getting more of this work for Canada. Now, what should and can be done?
Thirty years ago the government of Ontario introduced a plan which has been largely responsible for the spectacular expansion of the pulp and paper industry in that province during the intervening years. It required companies to process in the province a far higher proportion of the logs which they cut, a large proportion of which they had been shipping in the raw state to paper mills in the United States.
What has worked so well in the case of the pulp and paper industry in Ontario can work equally well in other primary industries right across the country. It should apply to all raw materials which we ship to other countries for further processing, and can succeed equally well because of the great dependence of other countries on our primary products to feed their manufacturing processes.
It is obvious that a certain proportion of the raw materials we produce must be exported in the raw state, but not nearly the proportion that is the case today. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should now undertake an intensive study of our primary industries to determine what proportion of the primary products we produce can reasonably be required to be processed to their finished state in this country.
Having decided what proportions of our various primary products should be further processed in Canada, we must produce an incentive which will be sufficiently attractive to persuade those who normally export our raw materials that it will be profitable for them to build the plants which will be necessary to carry out this additional processing in Canada.
It has become painfully obvious that the grants now provided by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, although useful, have not proved sufficiently attractive to bring to our areas of slow growth sufficient new industry to reverse the dangerously high rates of unemployment that have persisted in those areas for many years.
I believe that in addition to the DREE grants, which are now available to areas of slow growth, we must also make available an additional incentive in the form of a graduated scale of federal taxation which will permit a new plant processing primary products in an area of slow growth to pay no federal taxes in the first full year of profitable operation, and gradually increase its tax payments until it is paying full
[Mr. Philbrook.J
taxation in the fifteenth year. My conversations with leading businessmen across the country have convinced me that this incentive, added to the present DREE grants for slow growth areas, will prove sufficiently attractive to accomplish what has to be done.
The incentive which I have outlined will pay for itself many times over in the years ahead in the following ways: it will reduce the present far too high expenditure on unemployment insurance by stimulating the economy and enabling more people to find work. And we can increase tax revenues because (a), more people will be working and paying income taxes; (b) more commodities will be sold and will be raising additional commodity taxes; and (c), the increased volume of business will lower unit costs of production and make available more profits to tax.
In conclusion, the time is long overdue for us to stop shipping such a large proportion of our raw materials out of the country to provide jobs for other people. We must process a far higher proportion of them here in Canada for the benefit of Canadian production and employment.

These include the increase in the dividend tax credit from 33!6 per cent to 50 per cent beginning next year, the special inventory allowance of 3 per cent, and the extension of the investment tax credit.
The bill will also contribute to the small business sector by facilitating the expansion by Canadian-controlled private companies through joint ventures, business acquisitions, and plant replacement. Special provisions are contained for employee stock options and share purchase loans. These are designed to permit smaller companies to compete better in attracting managerial expertise. The Minister of Finance has further provided encouragement of funds for small business by the guarantee of capital gains treatment for investors and the special accommodation of provincial venture investment corporations.
These are steps taken by the minister and I know that they enjoy support from those opposite who have taken the trouble to acquaint themselves with these measures and their benefits.

I suppose I get even greater support for these measures from my friends opposite when I say this, and I know my colleague, the minister, would agree, that we must do more. I think as we go into this difficult year I want to try to convince my colleagues and other people in the community of the great importance of the creation of small business enterprises, particularly those of a high technology nature. I think it is clearly evidenced by the experience of the past that it is in these areas that enormous increases in employment can take place.
A study done in the United States some time ago contrasted the mature corporations, resource-oriented corporations, and high technology innovative corporations. For very heavy investment in the mature or resource based industries there was a very modest increase in hiring and employment. It showed what a dramatic effect can take place in a successful, innovative high technology type of company. Thousands were employed for a fraction of the investment in the other. 1 think the case can readily be made that the former minister of finance, given the circumstances he found himself in last spring and the circumstances his successor found himself in this fall, did the maximum possible to achieve the results we have.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we must look with new eyes, new sympathy, new enthusiasm on the small business sector. We must recognize that it is in this area that perhaps the greatest opportunities for the future and of Canada and its citizens lie.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) put his finger on the issue. It may well have been initiated for that purpose. I do not want to make a great issue of it because we will deal with it as time goes on, and history will also deal with it. It was introduced very hurriedly shortly after the minister took the portfolio. It was condemned out of hand by most of the business community.
I make these remarks, Mr. Speaker, because there is no one in this House who does not wish the minister success in his new portfolio, not as a minister but in terms of the segment of the economy which he is going to serve. I think it is important at the outset that he does not mislead the House, even though 1 think he did it in good fun. He had to be doing it in good fun, otherwise it would be deliberately misleading the House to say that Canadians are smiling because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is doing such a fine job. It may well be, as Canadians look upon this minister and the situation he inherited from another minister who is equally troubled in violent travail, that the facial expression he calls a smile is the result of a digestive upset when they contemplate the extent of the damage done to the economy.
It is not proper or right for the minister to say that other countries are in the same position. In his speech he relied heavily on the fact that the situation was equally confusing, difficult, and foreboding for the future of the United States as Canada, as if that were some solace to Canadians. More important, it is not in accordance with the facts, and the minister should know that.
In the United States there is less unemployment, less inflation, and twice the real growth rate of Canada. There is a trade surplus on current account in the United States compared to a trade deficit on current account in Canada. Not only do the words give no comfort to Canadians, they are not factual.
A minister embarking on his first speech should not delude himself. He should ask what small business wants. I can tell him some of the things I would like to see.
I talk to a lot of small businessmen in my constituency. They would like certain stability with respect to government policy, whether it is this minister's policy, that of the Minister of Finance, or of any other ministerial portfolio in the Government of Canada. They want to know there is a government in Ottawa which is concerned with small business. They want to know what is going to happen from one day to the next. The right hand should know what the left is doing, it has become painfully evident to me in the five years I have been here that this government does not know what it is doing.
The government's attack on problems is uncoordinated. Perhaps that is the reason why we find ourselves in this situation. Businessmen want a commitment from government.
Income Tax
They want a simple, ordinary, everyday service that is also provided to those who are not in business, namely, the operation of the mails.
I know solicitors, accountants, and many others who depend upon the mail for business. Today they cannot rely on Her Majesty's mail for the purpose of affecting a contract in the legal sense. As a result, this important service to business is being by-passed. They would like something of that nature.
They would like some co-ordination between provincial and federal business development programs. There is not very much at the moment. It is developing, but we have a long way to go in that regard.
These people want to be assured that when parliament debates small loans legislation or the new Federal Business Development Bank, as we did some time ago, that those agencies of government answer the needs of small business. They do not today. Government policy with regard to business is not related to the small business sector. It may come to be that way, but it is not that way now.
The minister issues press statements and uses brave words with regard to what he hopes for small business. However, there has to be some meat put on that skeleton. The minister must deal with his colleagues, which he has indicated will take some time. They do not quite understand him. I can understand why. It is not because the minister will not speak about it but because of the nature of the ministry. The problems of small business in this country must be addressed.
We do nothing but give lip service to the importance of small business as a place of employment. We owe more to the small businessman and the thousands of people looking for jobs in that sector which provides 50 per cent of the employment capacity in Canada. We must do more for them than merely utter small words.
I am honoured to follow in this debate the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) who, during his tenure of office as minister of trade and commerce, became the most energetic and productive member of any ministry in that period in that important portfolio.
What is left of our markets abroad? They have been affected in many ways by the policies of the government. What is left are the vestiges of those areas which were the beneficiaries of that hon. member's knowledge and ability.
I listened in absolute dismay to the speech by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook). I heard him say that small business needs more breaks, and that there is too little commitment to investment in Canada. A Liberal member of parliament said that tonight in this House. He sits on the back bench of the Liberal party. He said we need better industrial relations, that there is too much squabbling. Of course he is right.
What initiative did the government bring forward in the last session with regard to labour relations and an improvement in relations between employers and employees? There were none. The hon. member for Halton is absolutely right.

November 8, 1977
Income Tax
We have to find a better way than strikes. If there were a better way to deal with economic problems and problems between employers and employees, there is not a working man or woman in Canada who would not move in that direction, whether it be through labour courts, binding arbitration, or a host of other remedies that are available.
For the ten years that the government has been in power in Canada, more people have suffered from strikes. More have been engaged in strikes. This government sat on its butt and did absolutely nothing to meet with business and labour to find a way to bring the two sides together on some common ground. In that sense Ministers failed. They failed because they are tired, irritable, and more concerned about their own position than about those elements of society which cry out for some form of leadership. I am talking about the men and women who carry the lunch pails, the members of the work force in Canada. There is not a working person anywhere who wants to strike.
Government members have made great speeches about what they are going to do, about the great conferences they will hold and the seminars they will fund. However, we have a strike record in Canada that is second only to Italy. Of course, we need a better way.
The Liberal member for Halton pointed out that businessmen are worried about GATT. Of course they are worried about it. What is the position of this government? Is it to go out in the world as a Boy Scout and fight for absolute free trade? What is it going to do for the shoe manufacturer or the textile worker? What is its position with respect to GATT?
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) says one thing, the Minister of Finance says another, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), like a philosopher king, presides over that kind of disorder. Businessmen in Canada are asking the government where they stand. They want to know what position the government is taking in the world. They ask how the government is meeting opposition from other countries whose businesses and industries are subsidized or supported by government in a way that affects their basic ability to compete. These are some questions to which the ministry should address itself.
The hon. member for Halton talked about the necessity of long-range planning. I did not know that Liberal member is a closet socialist, but I guess he is. We in Canada would be satisfied with some short-range planning. At present we have no planning at all. Even some short-range policy-making would be of assistance.
Whether it is with regard to energy, industry or what have you, we talk about strategies. We do not talk about plans to develop. We move from band-aid to band-aid, while the country jolts from difficulty to difficulty. The government of the day, which asked for and received a mandate from the people in 1974, produced this so-called mini-budget, and now Bill C-ll. It is inadequate to meet the difficulties that face the country.

The hon. member went on to talk about science and technology. We in Canada have really stripped ourselves bare. The science and research community in Canada do not really ask for very much. They have asked the government to give them something so that we can develop our own technology rather than continue to be borrowers of technology as we have done over the past few years. They ask that the grants be stable so that they can count on them, because they must priorize their projects. There has been no stability in this very fundamental area.
No one knows me as a pessimist but let us get to what the Minister of State (Small Business) said about his Minister of Finance and his predecessor. By the end of 1977 Canadians will have experienced four years of inflation higher than 7 per cent, three years of unemployment at or higher than 7 per cent, four years of economic ruin below our 5 per cent growth potential, three years of trade deficits higher than $4 billion, and five years in which the federal budgetary deficit has increased. That is what we shall have experienced by the end of this year.
The hon. member for Halton said we wanted small, clean, streamlined government. I think Canadians would be prepared to settle for a government perhaps not quite so clean and perhaps not so streamlined, but reasonably responsive to the conditions we face today.
What does the minister offer us? After all the euphemisms used by speakers on the other side, all he can offer Canadians in 1978 is an inflation rate of 6 per cent, real economic growth of 5 per cent, and even larger federal debts. The Minister of Finance refuses to give us any forecasts, but that, in essence, is what we are offered.
We have a lot of things to concern ourselves about in this country in economic terms, but I am convinced, now, and I do not like to say it, that this government has proven itself so inept that we can expect nothing from it. It has lost its fighting spirit. The ministers have ceased to be responsive in a political sense to the needs of the country. They behave more like a board of directors, insensitive to the shareholders. That is the situation in which we find ourselves and, over-all, that is the economic situation in which we find ourselves.
I am concerned that we have young men and women in Canada crying out for work, men and women who have qualified themselves because we as a nation have said to them, "Go and get an education because the world will then be your oyster." We find them today up against the reality of a situation where their skills and learning cannot be used; they not only waste their lives but they cannot and do not make a contribution to their country.
I refuse to believe that this country, properly led, with the tremendous resources in human and material terms at its disposal, with an educational system that we tout as being the second-best in the world, sitting beside a large market, and with a tradition of exporting our goods, must look forward to the stagnation and gloom which the minister has predicted. If
November 8, 1977

the government continues to adopt the attitude that only it can do things, that its job is to do things for people, rather than create an atmosphere in which people can do things for themselves, then should it continue in office the Minister of Finance is absolutely right. That is precisely what we face-a bleak future.

When they are given an opportunity they can make what comments they wish in the course of their remarks. If they go to their constituencies and ask what their constituents really think of this government in terms of economic leadership, or if they go to the small business community and ask what businessmen think of this government as the great helper of small business, I think they will find that the euphemisms about Canadians smiling because they have the Minister of Finance at the controls are not true at all.
1 have always found that when I am getting pretty close to the truth members on the other side begin to wake up and shift in their seats as they are doing now. I can understand them. If 1 were over on the other side tonight, if 1 had to answer for the economic policies of the government, 1 would feel the same sense of discomfort as members obviously do on the other side.
The government is not completely unresponsive, though, 1 must say that. I recall reading the defence the minister put out of the new government policy to change the rules in midstream with respect to the taxation of benefits from insurance policies, a proposal which created such a hue and cry among the 12 million life insurance policy holders in Canada. Those life insurance policies represent, in many respects, aside from the home, perhaps, the most important form of saving for the future in which a family engages.
When the ministry dealt with this matter it decided to withdraw the death tax. I could not believe it. 1 could not believe they were at last retreating from the position which successive governments had taken, namely, that of imposing a death tax, increasing death duties whether upon insurance policies or by way of estate duties or otherwise. But the government tried it. There was a hue and cry. The issue was raised in the House, and I am sure it was raised in the Liberal caucus. The government decided it would be wise to back off.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) wrote to the Minister of Finance on September 21, 1977, putting forward the position of the official opposition with respect to the
Income Tax
matter. As a result, the government decided to withdraw, pending further study, the proposals which would have made taxable a portion of the investment income from certain life insurance policies realized on death. The remaining proposals, announced in the minister's statement, relate to the taxation of policy holders other than on the death of the insured, and these are now included in the measure which we are being asked to pass. What they have done with respect to the 12 million life insurance policy holders in Canada is this: they have changed in midstream the rules with respect to their rights and benefits in respect to these policies. The government has brought in a new form of taxation.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who is experienced in the field of insurance, indicated last night what it means to the average person who may decide to use proceeds from an insurance policy to finance a business or suchlike. For years and years members of the Canadian public who were holders of insurance policies have had certain rights. The government has now decided, without notice, to take those rights and benefits away from them. If a policy holder takes a loan on his policy and then has to pay a capital gains tax on that loan, if he then pays the loan back he does not regain the capital gains tax paid. In addition, he cannot use the interest charged by the company as a deduction against his income tax when that loan is used for financial purposes. For some reason or other, a man who takes a loan from an insurance company rather than a bank loses that deduction. This means that policy holders will have to go to the bank to borrow money, using the policy as collateral. It means, in effect, that policy holders will pay higher rates of interest at the bank, losing their advantageous interest rate from the insurance company.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka put it very well last night. He said that policy holders with long standing policies could borrow money against their policies at a rate not exceeding 7 per cent, whereas if they went to the bank today they would have to pay 12 per cent. The government should think about this. Liberal members do not speak up in the House, but they should certainly raise this matter in caucus.

We have been asking the government, year after year, to consider the urgent need to ease the great burden on Canadian taxpayers so far as residential taxes are concerned. They are not allowed to deduct at least part of these taxes, and this creates a kind of double taxation. Not only are taxpayers taxed heavily, as 1 have said, but they are the victims of double taxation.
it is my view, which I believe is shared by many people in this country, that those who dwell in owner-occupied homes, and tenants of rooming houses and apartment houses, deserve favourable consideration in this regard on the part of the Minister of Finance. 1 thought that when the minister brought

forward his mini-budget he would have thought of these people, but he did not. The federal government has a stake in the provision of adequate housing for its citizens, the creation of incentives to increase employment, and the lending of money to municipalities which must provide many services to their residents. Since federal government involvement in our cities is limited by the constitution, provincial governments are mostly responsible for land use planning, regional economic planning, and education.
In Canada, use of federal taxation power lays into the hands of the federal government an opportunity to help the property owner. As I have said, the person who pays property taxes in effect pays a double tax. The hard earned money with which Canadians pay their property taxes has already been taxed to death by the provincial and federal governments, not to mention the municipal governments. Many tax experts have described municipal residential taxes as inequitable and regressive, and I rather think they are right. They bear heavily on those who can least afford them.
At the present time property taxes paid by businessmen are deductible. Property taxes paid by apartment owners are deductible. Property taxes on single family homes rented to tenants are also deductible by the owners. Furthermore, an apartment building owner can take advantage of the corporate tax law and deduct his operating expenses, whereas dwellers in owner-occupied homes, tenants in boarding houses and apartment buildings, do not get any such relief in computing their federal income tax.
Not only are cities plagued with rising costs to meet the demands for more services, increased welfare payments and public works to provide jobs, but the ordinary citizen has been hard pressed with rising taxes at the federal, provincial, and especially the municipal level.
I have been quoting Hansard for February 26, 1971, Mr. Speaker, a proposition advanced by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). This is a proposition which has been supported in this House by Progressive Conservative members. Again in 1973 I joined in the debate and asked the government if it would consider this form of tax relief-because that is what is needed. To date, Mr. Speaker, even in what has been described as the mini-budget, the government has failed to act. It has failed to grant this tax relief to a segment of society for whom relief should be granted in order to assist in stimulating Canada's construction industry. I cannot understand why the government has refused this request.
What has the government done to assist in this matter? It has announced a $350 grant in Ontario, I think $500 in other parts of Canada, to upgrade insulation in houses. It has told Canadians to insulate their homes and has offered them $350. But what it has forgotten to tell Canadians, though it did put it in small print, is that they are going to be taxed on that grant. The grant becomes part of their taxable incomes.

That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. There are a host of other areas where the government has taken this kind of midstream approach. Is it any wonder that I said at the outset of my speech, through you to the Minister of State (Small Business) that what Canadian businessmen want in order to provide jobs is a better business and investment climate. Part of this climate is stability. But the business communities and other communities in Canada who depend upon the government for leadership do not have confidence that there is stability in government. In fact what is happening is that Canadians in all walks of life are looking at the government and asking themselves: by what right can it be said that it still has a mandate to lead?
The Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) announced the other day that he had come to the realization that the key to saving Canada was a sound economic climate. Yet when the government had an opportunity, at the beginning of this session, to bring in a budget, what did it do? It brought in a band-aid, instead of looking to the structures of our economic society to see where they could be changed, improved, and enhanced. We had this government giving with one hand and taking away with another. There is not a member on the other side of the House of Commons who is not ashamed of what the Minister of Finance did in this House of Commons.
The government has indicated that it wants this taxation bill passed quickly. It is important for members to know, and for the country to know, that we are not just debating the ministerial statement made a few nights ago in the House of Commons. We are only on the second day of the bill arising out of that. We are debating the budget of March 31, 1977, which announced all kinds of legislation that the government never saw fit to bring in, even though parliament was sitting for most of the summer.
When ministers stand in their places and state that members of parliament, who have been denied an opportunity for a general discussion of the government's economic program which a budget would allow, are under an obligation to pass quickly this piece of legislation, which is actually half a loaf, then I think the government had better think twice. Members of parliament were denied the rights and privileges of a budget

debate, and that is well known in the country. They were legally denied it, but slickly or politically denied it. Members of parliament are entitled to the opportunity for comment on the economic posture of the country and the government as it affects their constituencies.
It is our intention to use this debate to examine, hopefully for the benefit of the minister and hopefully for the benefit of the economic growth and welfare of the country, what Bili C-ll means; what the government's programs mean in terms of the country; and how they have failed. This is in the hope that the government will change its mind and realize that granting only three of the matters raised by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, and not the six major items proposed, is not satisfactory to us, nor is it satisfactory to the country, and I suspect it is not satisfactory to a good number of government backbenchers.
I am glad the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) is present in the Chamber. Perhaps he will understand the course this debate is taking. While we would not for one moment put any unnecessary impediment in the way of the passage of the bill, it is our intention to allow parliament the opportunity to debate this bill fully.

I presume the bills would all go out a little faster and people would pay a little faster, if they have the money with which to pay. Unfortunately this is the kind of advice and speeches small businesses hear at annual conventions and chamber of commerce meetings, and this is the kind of thing they start to believe in, to their own detriment.
Small businesses are willing to pay $2 and $3 to couriers to deliver letters. Yet they are not willing to give the Post Office two cents more in order to get adequate postal service. They pay 12 cents to send a letter, and they complain. They compare a 12-cent letter with service for which they are paying a courier $3. If they pay the Post Office two or three cents more, 15 cents a letter, they could get better service than any courier service could provide. But that is not a government enterprise, and one must not have a successful government enterprise!
Neither the Liberals nor the official opposition want a successful government enterprise because that would give the lie to the cry that private enterprise does everything better. However, that is an aside. 1 simply use it as an example to show how people get caught up in simplistic solutions which really do not relate to the problems.
Let me talk about the situation in Sudbury. Again the assumption is that you must stimulate small business in some direct way and that that is the answer. The truth of the matter is that while small businesses deserve to be helped, as do other elements of society, small businesses cannot be prosperous when there are almost a million people unemployed. You do not set out just to save small businesses; you set out to do something about the economy and to get people back to work, because if people are not working small businesses will not be prosperous, no matter what this government does and no matter what the official opposition might do if it were the government.
Let us take a look at the Sudbury situation where 1NCO laid off a number of people, at the Falconbridge lay-offs, and the lay-offs in other places. How are we going to help small business in Sudbury? The best way is to get those who are being laid off back to work. Otherwise, the whole downtown and most of the firms there are going to be in serious trouble. I am not talking just about retailers; 1 am talking about welders, electricians, maintenance people, and all the people who are associated with small companies which provide services. That is really what small businesses do; they provide specialized and highly personal services to some of the larger corporations. You cannot save small businesses in isolation. You cannot bring in policies for small businesses in isolation, without doing something about the economy generally.
Let us go back a number of years. It is unfortunate that small businesses have not seen the importance and value of what democratic socialists have done in this country. I remember years and years ago talking to many of my colleagues in small businesses, and they were complaining and unhappy because they had people working for them but their businesses were too small to have their own pension schemes. They knew that some of the loyal people who had been with them years and years would not have pensions, and one of the great things that saved them, and one of the great joys small employers experienced, was the beginning of the Canada Pension Plan.

Sure, a large company can put in a pension scheme, but how does a small company do that? They have to depend on a government scheme in order to do something decent for their employees. Most small businessmen are decent people who want to do it. Old age pensions were the same. They could not make provision for them by paying the premiums the insurance companies wanted in order to provide a decent retirement pension. And what happens with the labour code and minimum wages is Gresham's law-the bad employer drives out the good employer. A decent employer welcomes labour codes and minimum wages because it means that his competitors have to be as decent as he is himself.
If you talk to small businessmen they complain about government interference, but ask a man who has seriously thought about it if he wants to go back to the days when he did not have old age pension, Canada Pension Plan, medical services and hospital insurance programs for his employees. Even with all the complaints about unemployment insurance, do they want to go back to a time when they laid a man off and he had to go on welfare rather than being able to collect unemployment insurance? It is the conventional wisdom to be critical of all these things as an imposition on small business, yet the intelligent, decent, small businessman would not do without them.
Let us look at unemployment insurance in another way. Aside from the personal benefits that accrue to the person being laid off, many small businessmen could not maintain a labour force without unemployment insurance. Very often unemployment insurance is a greater boon to the business than it is to the employees who are laid off.
If we take what is happening in the economy at the moment, this serious recession, the terrible mismanagement, the perversity of government policies, and if that $4 billion that is coming out of the unemployment insurance were not being pumped back into the economy, what would happen to small business? Suppose the unemployment insurance payments were not being made in the depressed areas of Canada where unemployment is reaching close to 16 and 17 per cent, you would have a wave of bankruptcies in small business. It is the only thing that is sustaining those areas at the moment, this terrible socialistic policy.
It is the conventional wisdom to be against these things. There are abuses in all systems; nothing is perfect. I would be the last to claim we should not be trying to improve these measures, but the truth of the matter, from my observation, is that were it not for the so-called socialist measures we would be undergoing a depression that would make that of the thirties look pale. The chief victims would be the small businessmen of Canada who depend on the immediate purchasing power of the people.
It seems to me that whether or not hon. members agree with my general statement, if you place the arguments that I am putting forward against the solutions being offered by the government side-let us get rid of forms and we would have prosperity, and then improve the Post Office according to the

When I look at the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), 1 am reluctant to be rough with him. He is a very decent chap. Everybody likes him. I am sure he means well. I feel for him as I felt for his predecessor. What a rotten thing to do to a nice guy, make him Minister of Finance and saddle him with the insanities of the preceding policies of that government, expecting him to put a good face on it. At the moment, he is carrying it off.
He is a new minister. There is a sort of will on the part of the public to want to believe that perhaps this man will be able to do something the others were not able to do. It has driven more than one minister into exile. One got out completely. The other decided that he needed to go back to his family. I do not blame him for that.
I do not know where this minister will go. He has turned down the leadership of the Quebec Liberals. After a few months in the office of Minister of Finance, being leader of the Quebec Liberals might look very attractive. In any event, we wish him well. We are not saying things about the minister with malice. We know these are difficult times, not only in Canada but in other countries of the western world. We do not want to say they and they alone did it.
What I can be critical about is not that a miracle has not taken place in that the old budget plus the new mini-budget are just perverse and will do no good. In fact they may do a lot of harm. Therefore, whether we pass this measure or not is of no concern to me. In fact I think the greatest mercy we could show the country would be to make sure it does not pass. However, it will pass. But it is not worth passing because it is dangerous and damaging.
What is disturbing is that this kind of realization is not sinking in. Every once in a while the minister comes upon a piece of truth. The other day he said we may be saving too much, and just left it hanging in the air. We are saving too much, but whose fault is it? It is the fault of the government.
Who brought in registered retirement plans, incentives for savings, depreciation allowances, and the 5 per cent forgiveness of one kind or another? Who is continuing this policy? These are policies designed to increase savings. However, the minister says we are saving too much. I agree. We are saving ourselves right into a depression.
Does the minister do anything about it? Is he doing anything about it through the budget? The people who receive the benefits of the registered retirement savings plans are not the

poor. It is the better off, middle class and upper class, who are getting the chief benefits.
Businesses have more savings than they need. They do not know what to do in terms of investment. Why not save? They cannot spend it. There is a limit to how much a person can eat, how many cars he can drive, and how many washing machines he can own. But those who need it have not got it. Even the tax saving being proposed is for people with taxable incomes.
What about those who do not have taxable incomes? This is the great dichotomy, the reason we cannot get out of this terrible situation. Those who do not need to spend any more are getting the benefits of savings. Those who have great needs and would spend if they had it, are getting no benefit at all.
Unless we get a redistribution of income from those who have the money to those who do not, so that there will be more spending as a result of these tax cuts, it will simply result in it being socked away in the bank. The banks cannot even get more of their money out.
What is the consequence? Who is going to invest? Why give business more money? In what will they invest? They are only using 80, 82 or 83 per cent of their plant capacity now.

The kind of budget we are being asked to pass as quickly as possible for the sake of the country does not even hint at these problems. The foreign ownership chickens are coming home to roost. I listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) and the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees). They both made a number of points which were well worth noting. The hon. member for Halton raised the question of what happens as a consequence of foreign ownership.
The great benefits of foreign ownership are felt in the early stages. There is a lot of investment to begin with, but as soon as things get tough in the home country the gears are thrown into reverse. 1 am not condemning foreign ownership for taking this approach. That is the way things operate. We would do it ourselves. In fact we do have a Canadian company which is mining for nickel in Asia. Because miners are being laid off in this country, we say, "Stop mining for nickel in Asia and mine it in our own country because there is unemployment here." It is a natural tendency for any governing body to say in such circumstances, "Come home. Bring your jobs home.
It is natural in the United States, which is also faced with large scale unemployment, to say to its multinational corporations, "We do not want you investing your money around the world. That is fine so long as we do not need jobs here. But we do need jobs at home now and we want you to invest back here". This is precisely what is happening, Mr. Speaker. You see it happening with the Canada-U.S. auto agreement. In the initial stages Canada was reaping considerable benefit in terms of the number of jobs created in this country versus the number of automobiles purchased in this country. But in the last number of years the situation has been reversing itself and we are now running a serious deficit with the United States, if you include parts and finished cars.
If you look at the figures in the Auditor General's report showing what is happening to skilled jobs in the automobile industry, the same pattern emerges. The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) should be grateful for this: we are becoming the hewers of wood and drawers of water when it comes to making automobiles. The skilled jobs are going to the United States. We will be facing a serious situation unless something is done about it.
What we need is an industrial strategy. Today my leader issued a press release in which he said that we have to come to grips with an industrial strategy in the field of textiles, shoes.
